scenes.tts: Here is a puzzle. The tip of a growing axon is a flat fan, and the actin inside it is never still. Slice through it and look from the side. New actin joins the filaments at the front edge. Motor proteins called myosin two pull the whole network back toward the centre. So how does the edge ever move forward?
scenes.visual: Top-down fan slices into a side view; teal new actin enters at the front, red myosin pull sends the network back, a question mark at the unmoving edge.
scenes.caption: Here is a puzzle. The tip of a growing axon is a flat fan, and the actin inside it is never still. Slice through it and look from the side. New actin joins the filaments at the front edge. Motor proteins called myosin II pull the whole network back toward the centre. So how does the edge ever move forward?
scenes.narration: Here is a puzzle. The tip of a growing axon is a flat fan, and the actin inside it is never still. Slice through it and look from the side. New actin joins the filaments at the front edge. Motor proteins called myosin II pull the whole network back toward the centre. So how does the edge ever move forward?

scenes.tts: That backward movement is called retrograde flow. The network treadmills. Actin is added at the front and carried back at the same rate, so the edge goes nowhere. Think of the actin network as a running engine, and the surface under it, the substrate, as the road. The engine runs, but the car stays put.
scenes.visual: Red flow arrows and treadmilling dashes; added equals carried back; a marker shows the edge staying put; engine and road labels.
scenes.narration: That backward movement is called retrograde flow. The network treadmills. Actin is added at the front and carried back at the same rate, so the edge goes nowhere. Think of the actin network as a running engine, and the surface under it, the substrate, as the road. The engine runs, but the car stays put.

scenes.tts: Now add a clutch. When adhesion molecules link the actin network to the substrate, the clutch engages. Retrograde flow slows. The same actin addition now pushes the edge forward. Tim Mitchison and Marc Kirschner proposed this in 1988. It is called the clutch hypothesis.
scenes.visual: Yellow adhesion links appear under the network; flow arrows shorten and the edge crosses the marker.
scenes.narration: Now add a clutch. When adhesion molecules link the actin network to the substrate, the clutch engages. Retrograde flow slows. The same actin addition now pushes the edge forward. Tim Mitchison and Marc Kirschner proposed this in 1988. It is called the clutch hypothesis.

scenes.tts: Put it as a rule. The rate of advance equals the rate of actin addition at the edge, minus the rate of retrograde flow. With the clutch off, flow matches addition, and advance is zero. With the clutch on, flow falls, and advance rises.
scenes.visual: The equation builds in colour; three bars show addition, flow and advance as the clutch switches off then on.
scenes.narration: Put it as a rule. The rate of advance equals the rate of actin addition at the edge, minus the rate of retrograde flow. With the clutch off, flow matches addition, and advance is zero. With the clutch on, flow falls, and advance rises.

scenes.tts: Actin makes the advance. Microtubules make it permanent. Microtubules are hollow tubes that fill the centre of the growth cone. Once the edge has moved and the actin ahead has cleared, microtubules extend into the new territory. The fan behind them narrows, and that stretch becomes axon shaft.
scenes.visual: Purple microtubules grow forward behind the advancing edge; the fan behind them narrows into shaft.
scenes.narration: Actin makes the advance. Microtubules make it permanent. Microtubules are hollow tubes that fill the centre of the growth cone. scenes.tts: Now see how a growth cone turns. If advance is a balance at the edge, turning is a difference in that balance between the two sides. A cue on one side shifts actin assembly, flow or adhesion there. Gundersen and Barrett placed a pipette releasing nerve growth factor near chick sensory neurons. The growth cones turned toward it. Drugs released onto one side of a growth cone give simple results. Remove actin on one side, and the growth cone turns away from that side. Keep the rule. Advance is addition minus flow. Turning is the difference between sides.
scenes.visual: Top-down growth cone with a green advance arrow on each side; unequal arrows bend its path toward a cue, then away from the side with no actin; the rule is written.
